subject: ela
skillName: Ask and answer about a speaker

items.prompt:
A classmate says: 'I have a pet rabbit named Cotton.' What is a good question to get MORE information?
A) 'What did you eat for breakfast?'
B) 'What does Cotton eat?'

steps: Option B asks for new information about the rabbit the classmate mentioned. Option A is off-topic.

items.prompt:
A speaker uses a word you do not understand. What should you do?
A) Ignore it
B) Ask the speaker to explain the word
items.answer: B) Ask the speaker to explain the word

steps: If a speaker uses an unfamiliar word, asking for clarification is the right approach.

items.prompt:
True or False: A good question after a speaker should be connected to what the speaker said.
A) True
B) False

steps: Questions about a speaker should relate to the speaker's topic — either to clarify or gather more information.

items.prompt:
A teacher says: 'We will mix baking soda and vinegar together. When you pour the vinegar in, watch carefully.' A student asks: 'What will happen when they are mixed?' 
Is this a clarifying question or a more-information question?
A) Clarifying
B) More information

steps: Nothing the teacher said was unclear. The student wants to know the outcome — a detail the teacher has not yet shared.

items.prompt:
A classmate presents about insects. He says: 'Insects have six legs and three body parts.' A student asks: 'What are the three body parts called?' 
Why is this a good question?
A) Because it changes the topic.
B) Because it asks for a specific detail from what the speaker said.
items.answer: B) Because it asks for a specific detail from what the speaker said.

steps: The speaker stated there are three body parts but did not name them. The question asks for those specific names — a good detail-gathering question.

items.prompt:
A student asks a question that the speaker already answered during her presentation. What does this suggest?
A) The student was not listening carefully.
B) The student has excellent listening skills.
items.answer: A) The student was not listening carefully.

steps: Asking a question that was already answered indicates the student was not paying full attention to the presentation.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Rainforests cover only about 6% of Earth's surface but contain more than 50% of all plant and animal species in the world.' A student asks: 'Why does such a small area of the Earth have so many different species?' 
Analyze why this is an excellent question.
items.answer: It is excellent because: (1) the student used two specific facts from the speech (6% of surface, 50%+ of species) and noticed a surprising contrast; (2) the question asks for an explanation of WHY, which the speaker did not provide; (3) it requires deeper reasoning about a relationship implied in the statistics.

steps: The student identified a paradox in the speech: small area, huge biodiversity.
The speaker stated the statistics but did not explain the reason.
Asking 'why' targets the logical gap in the speech — a high-quality inferential question.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a clarifying question and a more-information question? Use the speaker statement 'Sharks can smell blood from far away' to give an example of each.
items.answer: Clarifying question: 'How far exactly is 'far away'? I wasn't sure what distance that meant.' More-information question: 'How does a shark's sense of smell work — does it use its nose?' Clarifying removes confusion about something stated; more-information extends the topic with a new detail not yet provided.

steps: Clarifying: targets an unclear or vague part of what was said ('far away' is vague).
More information: asks for a new detail the speaker has not yet shared (how shark smell works).
Both are connected to the speaker's topic.
